cards.q: What happens when kernel-mode code crashes?
cards.a: The whole machine stops with a bug check (blue screen), because there is nothing above the kernel to recover.
cards.lessonTitle: User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different

cards.q: How does user-mode code get something done that only the kernel can do?
cards.a: It makes a system call, which switches the processor to kernel mode to run trusted code on its behalf.
cards.lessonTitle: User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different

cards.q: Why must all driver testing happen in a virtual machine?
cards.a: A driver bug can crash or corrupt the whole system; in a virtual machine that costs a snapshot restore, not your work.
cards.lessonTitle: User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different

cards.q: Why does the VM need more than one virtual processor?
cards.a: Many synchronisation bugs only appear when code really runs on several processors at the same time.

cards.q: Where is test signing turned on, and why only there?
cards.a: Only in the target VM: it is a development setting that lets test-signed drivers load, appropriate for a machine that exists to be crashed.

cards.q: What does the kernel debugger do when the target crashes?
cards.a: It stops at the bug check before the blue screen, so you can analyse the crash with commands such as !analyze -v.

cards.q: What is the difference between WDM and KMDF?
cards.a: WDM is the underlying driver model; KMDF is a framework on top of it that handles much of the boilerplate correctly.

cards.q: In what unit is UNICODE_STRING's Length measured?
cards.a: In bytes, not characters, and without any terminating null.

cards.q: How do you test whether an NTSTATUS means success?
cards.a: NT_SUCCESS(status), which is true for status >= 0.

cards.q: What happens if a driver does not set DriverUnload?
cards.a: It cannot be unloaded; it stays until the machine restarts.

cards.q: What must DriverEntry do before returning a failure status?
cards.a: Undo everything it already did, because Unload will not be called for a driver that failed to load.

cards.q: Why is a callback left registered after unload so dangerous?
cards.a: The kernel keeps calling an address where the driver's code no longer exists, which crashes the machine.

cards.q: Why does WinDbg need the driver's .pdb file?
cards.a: It holds the symbols: function names, types and source lines for the driver's code.

cards.q: What does bug check 0xD1 usually mean?
cards.a: Code at a raised IRQL touched pageable or invalid memory.

cards.q: What is the difference between bp and bu?
cards.a: bu sets a breakpoint by name that is resolved when the module loads, so it works before the driver is loaded.

cards.q: Why does a driver create a symbolic link?
cards.a: User mode cannot open names under \Device; the link in \?? makes the device reachable as \\.\Name.

cards.q: What does IoCreateDeviceSecure add over IoCreateDevice?
cards.a: A security descriptor, so only the accounts it names (for example SYSTEM and Administrators) can open the device.

cards.q: In which order does Unload delete the link and the device?
cards.a: The reverse of creation: the symbolic link first, then the device object.

cards.q: What does IoStatus.Information usually hold?
cards.a: The number of bytes transferred, which user mode sees as the result of ReadFile or WriteFile.

cards.q: What happens if a driver never completes an IRP?
cards.a: The requesting thread waits forever, and its process cannot exit.

cards.q: Why must a driver not touch an IRP after IoCompleteRequest?
cards.a: The IRP may already be freed and reused; anything needed must be read before completing it.

cards.q: What does the access field of a control code do?
cards.a: The I/O manager checks that the handle was opened with that access before the request reaches the driver.

cards.q: Why do driver and client share one header?
cards.a: They must agree exactly on the control codes and the layout of the data they exchange.

cards.q: What does the user see as "bytes returned" from DeviceIoControl?
cards.a: The IRP's IoStatus.Information value set by the driver.

cards.q: With METHOD_BUFFERED, how big is the system buffer for an IOCTL?
cards.a: The larger of the input and output lengths; input and output share it.

cards.q: What does an MDL describe?
cards.a: The locked physical pages of a user buffer, which the driver maps into kernel space for direct I/O.

cards.q: Why is METHOD_NEITHER dangerous?
cards.a: The driver gets raw user addresses that may be invalid, point into the kernel, or change while being read; it must probe and capture everything itself.

cards.q: Why must count * size checks be written as count > room / size?
cards.a: The multiplication can overflow and wrap to a small number that passes the check; the division cannot.

cards.q: What is a double-fetch bug?
cards.a: Reading a user-controlled value twice, so it can change between the check and the use.

cards.q: Why set Information to 0 when failing a request?
cards.a: So no uninitialised kernel bytes are copied back to user mode.

cards.q: When must a driver use non-paged pool?
cards.a: When the memory is touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above, for example in a DPC or while holding a spin lock.

cards.q: Why does the tag 'nriC' show up as Cirn in PoolMon?
cards.a: A multi-character constant is stored little-endian, so its characters appear in reverse order in memory.

cards.q: Why is a big local array dangerous in a driver?
cards.a: Kernel stacks are only about 12 KB; a large local can overflow the stack and crash the machine.

cards.q: Why can code at DISPATCH_LEVEL not wait?
cards.a: The scheduler cannot run on that processor, so there is nothing to switch to while waiting.

cards.q: Why can code at DISPATCH_LEVEL not touch paged memory?
cards.a: If the page is not resident, the page fault needs to wait for the disk, which is impossible at that level.

cards.q: How do you find the highest IRQL at which a function may be called?
cards.a: The IRQL line at the end of its documentation (and its _IRQL_requires_max_ annotation).

cards.q: Why must spin locks be held only briefly?
cards.a: Other processors busy-wait for them at DISPATCH_LEVEL, wasting CPU and blocking that processor's scheduling.

cards.q: Which lock would you choose for data used by a DPC and a dispatch routine?
cards.a: A spin lock (preferably queued), because the DPC runs at DISPATCH_LEVEL where waiting is impossible.

cards.q: What does deadlock detection look for?
cards.a: A cycle in the order locks are acquired: lock A then B in one place, B then A in another.

cards.q: At which IRQL does a DPC run, and what does that forbid?
cards.a: DISPATCH_LEVEL: no waiting and no touching paged memory.

cards.q: What does a negative due time in KeSetTimerEx mean?
cards.a: A time relative to now, in 100-nanosecond units.

cards.q: Why must Unload call KeFlushQueuedDpcs after cancelling timers?
cards.a: A DPC may already be queued or running; flushing waits for it so it never runs in unloaded code.

cards.q: What does CONTAINING_RECORD do?
cards.a: Given the address of a LIST_ENTRY member, it computes the address of the structure that contains it.

cards.q: How do you know an intrusive circular list is empty?
cards.a: The head's Flink points to the head itself.

cards.q: Why are intrusive lists well suited to the kernel?
cards.a: Inserting and removing never allocate, so they cannot fail and work under a spin lock.

cards.q: What does a null PPS_CREATE_NOTIFY_INFO mean in the process callback?
cards.a: The process is exiting rather than being created.

cards.q: Why must notification callbacks be fast?
cards.a: They run synchronously in the creating or exiting thread, so every process and thread creation on the machine waits for them.

cards.q: Why are process ids alone not enough to identify a process in a log?
cards.a: Ids are reused after a process exits; the start time distinguishes processes that had the same id.

cards.q: Why should a driver rate-limit DbgPrintEx in hot paths?
cards.a: Formatting and printing are slow, and a message per event can flood the debugger and slow the whole system.
cards.lessonTitle: Logging and Tracing from a Driver

cards.q: What do levels and keywords let a trace session do?
cards.a: Enable only events of a given importance and area, so disabled events cost almost nothing.
cards.lessonTitle: Logging and Tracing from a Driver

cards.q: What advantage does ETW have over a private log?
cards.a: Its events appear in system-wide tools like WPA, on the same timeline as CPU, disk and other system events.
cards.lessonTitle: Logging and Tracing from a Driver

cards.q: Why does the read request carry afterSeq instead of the driver remembering each reader's position?
cards.a: The driver then keeps no per-reader state; readers are independent and a crashed viewer leaves nothing behind.

cards.q: Why is losing events preferable to blocking when the viewer is slow?
cards.a: Blocking would slow down or stop process creation for the whole system; losing old events only affects the log.

cards.q: What must Unload do first?
cards.a: Unregister the callbacks, so no new events arrive into memory that is about to be freed.

cards.q: How does special pool catch a buffer overrun at the moment it happens?
cards.a: Each allocation is placed right against an inaccessible guard page, so the first byte past the end faults.

cards.q: Why does Force IRQL checking make paged-memory bugs reproducible?
cards.a: It makes pageable memory non-resident whenever the IRQL is raised, so every bad access faults instead of only some.

cards.q: What does low resources simulation test?
cards.a: The failure paths after allocations, by making random allocations fail.

cards.q: What does _IRQL_requires_max_(DISPATCH_LEVEL) let analysis check?
cards.a: That the function is never called at an IRQL above DISPATCH_LEVEL.

cards.q: Why write driver logic as kernel-independent C++?
cards.a: So it can be unit-tested and fuzzed in user mode quickly, leaving only a thin kernel layer to review.

cards.q: What is the difference between generation and mutation fuzzing?
cards.a: Generation builds inputs from the protocol's description; mutation changes valid inputs randomly.

cards.q: Why is a generic "read memory at this address" IOCTL a serious flaw?
cards.a: It lets any program that can open the device read kernel memory, turning the driver into a tool against the whole system.

cards.q: What does FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN protect against?
cards.a: Opens of names under the device (\\.\Device\anything) that would otherwise skip the device's security check.

cards.q: Why should a driver never return kernel pointers to user mode?
cards.a: They reveal the kernel's memory layout, which helps attackers defeat address randomisation.

cards.q: Why can a developer's own certificate not sign a kernel driver for release?
cards.a: Since Windows 10 1607, release kernel drivers must be signed by Microsoft through the Partner Center.
cards.lessonTitle: Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver

cards.q: What does DriverVer in an INF decide?
cards.a: Which of several driver packages Windows prefers, by date and version.
cards.lessonTitle: Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver

cards.q: How could the log driver's information be obtained without a driver?
cards.a: By a user-mode program reading the kernel's ETW process and thread events.
cards.lessonTitle: Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver
